title: How to estimate your 1RM without maxing out
description: One hard set of a few reps can estimate your one-rep max, no max attempt needed. How to do it, where it misleads, and how to track it.
imageAlt: Abstract rising steps in Gymon's blue-grey, a placeholder image for this sample article
hook: Ever wondered what you could lift for a single rep? Good news: you don't have to find out the hard way.
bottomLine: One heavy set of a few reps can estimate your max, close enough to track your progress.

beats.heading: A heavy set already knows your max
beats.text: Put the weight and the reps into a simple formula, and out comes an estimate [[r2]]. No spotter, no drama, no testing day.

beats.heading: Light, long sets can flatter you
beats.text: People used to long sets squeeze out more reps at the same weight [[r1]]. In one small study, runners did about twice as many reps as lifters at 70% of their max [[r1]].

beats.heading: Heavier sets give steadier numbers
beats.text: The gap between people shrank as the weight went up [[r1]]. So pick a set that feels genuinely heavy, but still clean.

beats.heading: Watch the trend, not the number
beats.text: One estimate can wobble with a good or a bad day. The same lift, logged the same way each week, tells you if you are getting stronger.

pullQuote.lead: And one of the best-known formulas started life as…
pullQuote.text: A poundage chart, not based on scientific research.
pullQuote.attribution: Richens & Cleather (2014), on where the Epley formula came from

tips.heading: Try it this week
items: Pick a lift you already do, like a squat or a bench press.
Warm up, then do one heavy set of a few reps, and stop before your form slips.
Pop the weight and reps into the calculator below.
Repeat in a few weeks: same lift, same depth, same rest.

references.title: The relationship between the number of repetitions performed at given intensities is different in endurance and strength trained athletes
references.quote: Eight weightlifters and eight endurance runners each completed a one repetition maximum test on the leg press and completed repetitions to fatigue at 90, 80 and 70% of their one repetition maximum. The endurance runners completed significantly more repetitions than the weightlifters at 70% (39.9 ± 17.6 versus 17.9 ± 2.8; p < 0.05) and 80% (19.8 ± 6.4 versus 11.8 ± 2.7; p < 0.05) of their one repetition maximum but not at 90% (10.8 ± 3.9 versus 7.0 ± 2.1; p > 0.05) of one repetition maximum. … Epley [ 8 ] A poundage chart, not based on scientific research.
references.finding: Eight weightlifters and eight endurance runners lifted to failure at 70%, 80% and 90% of their leg-press max. Runners did far more reps at 70% (39.9 vs 17.9) and at 80%, but not at 90%.

references.title: Strength Testing—Predicting a One-Rep Max from Reps-to-Fatigue
references.venue: Journal of Physical Education, Recreation & Dance 64(1):88–90
